original_question: Resolve the celestial-mechanics problems asking whether a photon, or another particle already traveling at about 0.99 c, can be accelerated to a speed greater than c; whether a flexible bridge can be built between two planets despite their gravitational fields and continuing orbital motion; whether two pieces of a split planet would re-form or separate when the pieces are equal or unequal; why Earth is seen above from the Moon while the Moon is seen above from Earth; and how objects, elevators, ocean water, and Coriolis forces would behave in a tunnel that crosses the Earth, either through the center or off-center.
target_in_paper: Section 3.1, Some open problems in Celestial Mechanics, specifically the five open problems 3.1.1-3.1.5: Photon speed, Flexible bridge, Splitting planet, Seeing the Moon, and Tunnel into the Earth.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's actual target as the five-item list in Section 3.1 on celestial mechanics, and it preserves the main content of each item: the photon-or-0.99c speed question, the flexible bridge between planets with gravitational-field and orbital-motion issues, the split-planet equal-versus-unequal case, the Earth/Moon mutually-above visibility puzzle, and the Earth-tunnel questions about falling bodies, elevators, water, and Coriolis effects.
missing_details: The paper does not present these as one theorem or conjecture, but as five separately numbered open problems inside Section 3.1; that structural fact should be made explicit.

For 3.1.2, the paper explicitly asks about a smooth escape from the gravitational field of one planet and a smooth entry into the gravitational field of the other, not only the abstract existence of a bridge.
For 3.1.4, the hidden assumption is a fixed observation point on Earth and an analogous fixed point on the Moon; the question is framed in terms of horizon visibility from those fixed points.

For 3.1.5, the centered-tunnel case contains several distinct subquestions that your draft compresses: whether a dropped object oscillates through the center, whether it eventually stops, and whether it then floats at the center.

For 3.1.5, the elevator question is not just about behavior in the tunnel; it specifically asks how much force is needed to push a free-falling elevator up to the opposite surface, especially from the Earth's center, and whether inertial carry-through past the center occurs.
For 3.1.5, the paper separately asks whether a passenger in the free-falling elevator feels gravity, invoking the equivalence-principle issue for motion inside a rotating gravitating body.

For 3.1.5, the ocean-water question is more specific than your draft: if one tunnel mouth is at the bottom of an ocean, will water descend only to the center, pass lower toward the far side, balance about the center, or flood out the original side.

For 3.1.5, the off-center case is stated as repeating the previous three questions for a tunnel that does not pass through the Earth's center, plus asking whether the tunnel midpoint plays the role of the Earth's center and how Coriolis force changes the answer.

The paper gives no formal variables, equations, ambient ring/field, homogeneity condition, degree restriction, nilpotency assumption, or asymptotic quantifier; those notions are not applicable here because the target is an informal qualitative physics problem, not an algebraic statement.
refined_question: Consider the following five qualitative open problems in celestial mechanics and Earth dynamics: (1) is it possible to accelerate a photon, or any other particle already traveling at about 0.99 c, so that its speed exceeds c; (2) is it possible to construct a flexible bridge between two planets that would permit terrestrial traffic, while allowing a smooth escape from the gravitational field of one planet, a smooth entry into the gravitational field of the other, and accommodating the continuous motion of the planets; (3) if a planet were cut into two separated parts, would equal halves re-attract and reform a single planet or instead separate further, and what changes if one part is significantly larger than the other; (4) taking a fixed point on Earth from which the Moon is visible only when it is above the local horizon, and analogously a fixed point on the Moon from which Earth is visible, why is Earth seen above from the Moon while the Moon is also seen above from Earth; and (5) for a tunnel joining opposite sides of the Earth, first through the center and then in an off-center configuration, determine whether a dropped object oscillates through the center and eventually stops or floats there, how much force is needed to push a free-falling elevator from the center toward the far surface and whether inertia carries it beyond the center, whether passengers experience Coriolis effects or feel gravity during free fall, how ocean water behaves if one tunnel mouth lies at the bottom of an ocean, and whether in the off-center case the tunnel midpoint plays a role analogous to the Earth's center.
justification: The draft matches Section 3.1 of the paper almost line by line. Open problem 3.1.1 asks whether a photon, or another particle traveling at say 0.99 c, can be accelerated to a speed greater than c. Open problem 3.1.2 asks about constructing a flexible bridge between two planets, explicitly raising the issues of each planet's gravitational field and the planets' continuous motion. Open problem 3.1.3 asks what happens if a planet is cut into two separated parts, first when the parts are equal and then when one is significantly larger. Open problem 3.1.4 asks why Earth is seen above from the Moon while the Moon is seen above from Earth, with the nearby parenthetical remark giving the fixed-point horizon-visibility setup. Open problem 3.1.5 asks the tunnel-through-the-Earth questions, including falling objects, elevators, Coriolis effects, whether passengers feel gravity in free fall, water flow when one tunnel opening is at the bottom of an ocean, and repetition of the analysis for an off-center tunnel. Because your draft bundles exactly these five numbered items and not any neighboring subsection from 3.2 or Chapter 4, the most paper-faithful target is the entire five-part list in Section 3.1 rather than any single narrower subproblem.
